text:
Every SSD stores your data in NAND flash cells, and those cells wear out. TLC (triple-level cell) flash, the type used in most everyday drives, lasts roughly 3,000 write cycles per cell before it starts to degrade. That sounds like a short life, but the drive has two ways to work around it.

The first is wear leveling. The controller spreads writes evenly across every block so that no single cell wears out while the cells next to it sit unused. The second is over-provisioning, a hidden reserve of spare flash that's usually around 7% of the drive. The controller uses it to replace worn blocks and keep performance steady.

Together, these two features stretch those 3,000 cycles over years of normal use. Your photos, games, and work files are safe on a drive like this, and I think that's a pretty clever piece of engineering.
